title: The acute effect of carbohydrate supplementation with 60 grams of glucose on performance after and metabolic response during maximal strength-oriented resistance training with 90% of one repetition maximum – a randomized controlled crossover trial
summary: In endurance sports, carbohydrates consumed during exercise are known to help maintain performance for longer. Whether this also applies to heavy resistance training with high loads has been studied only to a limited extent. In this study we compare how such training with and without a carbohydrate drink affects performance, blood glucose and lactate, perceived exertion and muscle soreness. Adults aged 18 to 40 years with resistance training experience complete two training sessions with bench press, deadlift, row and leg extension. In one session they drink a beverage containing carbohydrates and in the other a beverage without carbohydrates. The order is determined by chance and participants do not know which drink they receive. Before, during and after training, blood glucose and lactate are measured from a drop of blood, and strength and jump tests are performed. On the first and second day afterwards, participants are asked about muscle soreness.
conditions: No diseases are investigated. The study is conducted in healthy, resistance-trained adults. It examines acute performance-related, metabolic and subjective responses to maximal strength-oriented resistance training depending on carbohydrate intake.

interventions.name: Carbohydrate drink. Participants complete a maximal strength-oriented resistance training session with bench press, deadlift, row and leg extension (4 sets of 4 repetitions each at 90% of one-repetition maximum, 4 minutes rest between sets, 3 minutes between exercises). During the session they drink
Placebo. Identical resistance training session as in group 1. During the session participants drink 500 ml of water containing 0.5 g citric acid and 0.5 g sodium chloride without carbohydrate.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
At least 1 year of resistance training experience
At least 2 resistance training sessions per week
Experience with free weight training
Voluntary participation and written informed consent
Full legal capacity and understanding of the nature, scope and consequences of the study
Exclusion criteria:
Metabolic diseases
Cardiovascular diseases
Musculoskeletal injuries or incompletely healed sports injuries
Medication affecting glucose metabolism
Acute illness or other health restrictions that do not allow safe participation in resistance training
